title: Hypothesis Testing
subtitle: ClipSAT Printable Practice Suite (clipsat.org) • Topic 15.01 • 20 FRQs + 25 MCQs • Difficulty Progression • Cross-Lesson Synthesis

sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: State the null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether a new fertilizer increases the mean crop yield $\mu$, given a historical mean $\mu_0=50$ kg. Classify the test as one-tailed or two-tailed.
questions.target: The logic of hypothesis testing
questions.answer: $H_0:\mu=50$. $H_a:\mu>50$. This is a one-tailed (right-tailed) test, since the alternative specifies a direction.
questions.explanation: $H_0:\mu=50$. $H_a:\mu>50$. This is a one-tailed (right-tailed) test, since the alternative specifies a direction.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a one-tailed and a two-tailed hypothesis test, giving an example scenario for each.
questions.target: The logic of hypothesis testing
questions.answer: A one-tailed test is used when the alternative hypothesis specifies a direction (e.g. testing whether a new drug \emph{increases} recovery rate). A two-tailed test is used when the alternative simply states the parameter differs from the claimed value, without specifying direction (e.g. testing whether a machine's mean output has changed at all, up or down).
questions.explanation: A one-tailed test is used when the alternative hypothesis specifies a direction (e.g. testing whether a new drug \emph{increases} recovery rate). A two-tailed test is used when the alternative simply states the parameter differs from the claimed value, without specifying direction (e.g. testing whether a machine's mean output has changed at all, up or down).

questions.q: A test has $H_0:\mu=75$ vs $H_a:\mu\neq75$, and the sample data leads to rejecting $H_0$ at the 5% significance level. State, without further calculation, whether this data would also lead to rejection at the 1% level, justifying your answer.
questions.target: The logic of hypothesis testing
questions.answer: Not necessarily — a stricter significance level (1%) requires stronger evidence (a smaller $p$-value) to reject $H_0$. If the $p$-value is very small (well below $0.01$), rejection would still occur at 1%; but if the $p$-value lies between $0.01$ and $0.05$, $H_0$ would be rejected at 5% but not at 1%.
questions.explanation: Not necessarily — a stricter significance level (1%) requires stronger evidence (a smaller $p$-value) to reject $H_0$. If the $p$-value is very small (well below $0.01$), rejection would still occur at 1%; but if the $p$-value lies between $0.01$ and $0.05$, $H_0$ would be rejected at 5% but not at 1%.

questions.q: A machine fills bags with a claimed mean of $500$g, with known population standard deviation $\sigma=15$g. A sample of $n=36$ bags has mean $\bar{x}=494$g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean is less than 500g, using $z=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ and critical value $-1.645$.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a population mean (known σ)
questions.answer: $z=\frac{494-500}{15/\sqrt{36}}=\frac{-6}{2.5}=-2.4$. Since $-2.4<-1.645$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill weight is less than $500$g.
questions.explanation: $z=\frac{494-500}{15/\sqrt{36}}=\frac{-6}{2.5}=-2.4$. Since $-2.4<-1.645$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill weight is less than $500$g.

questions.q: A population has known standard deviation $\sigma=8$. A sample of $n=64$ has mean $\bar{x}=103$, against a claimed mean $\mu_0=100$. Test at the 1% level whether the mean exceeds 100, using critical value $z^*=2.326$.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a population mean (known σ)
questions.answer: $z=\frac{103-100}{8/\sqrt{64}}=\frac{3}{1}=3$. Since $3>2.326$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 1% level that the mean exceeds $100$.
questions.explanation: $z=\frac{103-100}{8/\sqrt{64}}=\frac{3}{1}=3$. Since $3>2.326$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 1% level that the mean exceeds $100$.

questions.q: A standardized test historically has mean $\mu_0=100$ with $\sigma=15$. A sample of $n=25$ students taking a new prep course has mean $\bar{x}=107$. Test at the 5% level (two-tailed) whether the course changes the mean score, using critical values $\pm1.96$.
questions.target: Two-tailed tests for a population mean
questions.answer: $z=\frac{107-100}{15/\sqrt{25}}=\frac{7}{3}\approx2.333$. Since $|2.333|>1.96$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the prep course changes the mean score.
questions.explanation: $z=\frac{107-100}{15/\sqrt{25}}=\frac{7}{3}\approx2.333$. Since $|2.333|>1.96$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the prep course changes the mean score.

questions.q: Using $z\approx2.33$ from the previous problem, find the two-tailed $p$-value, given $\Phi(2.33)\approx0.9901$, and confirm the conclusion.
questions.target: Two-tailed tests for a population mean
questions.answer: $p\mathrm{-value}=2(1-\Phi(2.33))=2(1-0.9901)=2(0.0099)=0.0198$. Since $0.0198<0.05$, we reject $H_0$, confirming the earlier conclusion.
questions.explanation: $p\mathrm{-value}=2(1-\Phi(2.33))=2(1-0.9901)=2(0.0099)=0.0198$. Since $0.0198<0.05$, we reject $H_0$, confirming the earlier conclusion.

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: A sample of $n=50$ has mean $\bar{x}=48.2$, against a claimed mean $\mu_0=50$ with $\sigma=6$. Test at the 5% level (two-tailed) whether the mean differs from 50, using critical values $\pm1.96$.
questions.target: Two-tailed tests for a population mean
questions.answer: $z=\frac{48.2-50}{6/\sqrt{50}}=\frac{-1.8}{0.8485}\approx-2.121$. Since $|-2.121|>1.96$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean differs from $50$.
questions.explanation: $z=\frac{48.2-50}{6/\sqrt{50}}=\frac{-1.8}{0.8485}\approx-2.121$. Since $|-2.121|>1.96$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean differs from $50$.

questions.q: A website historically crashes at a rate of $\lambda_0=4$ per month. After a software update, 1 crash is observed in a randomly selected month. Test at the 5% level whether the crash rate has decreased, using $P(X\leq1)\approx0.0916$ for $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(4)$.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a Poisson mean
questions.answer: $H_0:\lambda=4$. $H_a:\lambda<4$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\leq1)=0.0916$. Since $0.0916>0.05$, we do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the crash rate has decreased.
questions.explanation: $H_0:\lambda=4$. $H_a:\lambda<4$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\leq1)=0.0916$. Since $0.0916>0.05$, we do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the crash rate has decreased.

questions.q: Explain why an exact Poisson probability, rather than a normal approximation, is used to test a hypothesis about a Poisson mean when $\lambda_0$ is small.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a Poisson mean
questions.answer: When $\lambda_0$ is small, the Poisson distribution is noticeably skewed and a normal approximation would be unreliable, so exact Poisson probabilities give a more accurate $p$-value.
questions.explanation: When $\lambda_0$ is small, the Poisson distribution is noticeably skewed and a normal approximation would be unreliable, so exact Poisson probabilities give a more accurate $p$-value.

questions.q: A call center historically receives calls at $\lambda_0=6$ per hour. During a promotional event, 12 calls are received in one hour. Test at the 5% level whether the call rate has increased, using $P(X\geq12)\approx0.0201$ for $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(6)$.
questions.target: Further Poisson mean tests
questions.answer: $H_0:\lambda=6$. $H_a:\lambda>6$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\geq12)=0.0201$. Since $0.0201<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased during the promotional event.
questions.explanation: $H_0:\lambda=6$. $H_a:\lambda>6$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\geq12)=0.0201$. Since $0.0201<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased during the promotional event.

questions.q: A factory's defect rate is historically $\lambda_0=3$ per shift. During a trial of new equipment, 8 defects are observed in one shift. Test at the 5% level whether the defect rate has increased, using $P(X\geq8)\approx0.0119$ for $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(3)$.
questions.target: Further Poisson mean tests
questions.answer: $H_0:\lambda=3$. $H_a:\lambda>3$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\geq8)=0.0119$. Since $0.0119<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the defect rate has increased.
questions.explanation: $H_0:\lambda=3$. $H_a:\lambda>3$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\geq8)=0.0119$. Since $0.0119<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the defect rate has increased.

questions.q: A company claims $40\%$ of its customers use its mobile app ($p_0=0.4$). In a sample of $n=15$ customers, 10 report using the app. Test at the 5% level whether the true proportion is greater than 40%, using $P(X\geq10)\approx0.0338$ for $X\sim B(15,0.4)$.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a binomial proportion
questions.answer: $H_0:p=0.4$. $H_a:p>0.4$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\geq10)=0.0338$. Since $0.0338<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that more than 40% of customers use the app.
questions.explanation: $H_0:p=0.4$. $H_a:p>0.4$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\geq10)=0.0338$. Since $0.0338<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that more than 40% of customers use the app.

questions.q: Explain why the binomial hypothesis test uses the exact binomial distribution rather than a normal approximation when $n$ is small.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a binomial proportion
questions.answer: For small $n$, the binomial distribution can be quite skewed (especially if $p_0$ is far from $0.5$), so a normal approximation would be unreliable; exact binomial probabilities give a more accurate $p$-value.
questions.explanation: For small $n$, the binomial distribution can be quite skewed (especially if $p_0$ is far from $0.5$), so a normal approximation would be unreliable; exact binomial probabilities give a more accurate $p$-value.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: A coin is tested for fairness ($p_0=0.5$). In 20 tosses, 6 heads are observed. Test at the 5% level (two-tailed) whether the coin is biased, using $P(X\leq6)\approx0.0577$ for $X\sim B(20,0.5)$ (doubled for a two-tailed test).
questions.target: Further binomial proportion tests
questions.answer: $H_0:p=0.5$. $H_a:p\neq0.5$. Two-tailed $p\mathrm{-value}=2\times P(X\leq6)=2(0.0577)=0.1154$. Since $0.1154>0.05$, we do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the coin is biased.
questions.explanation: $H_0:p=0.5$. $H_a:p\neq0.5$. Two-tailed $p\mathrm{-value}=2\times P(X\leq6)=2(0.0577)=0.1154$. Since $0.1154>0.05$, we do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the coin is biased.

questions.q: A politician claims $60\%$ of voters support a new policy ($p_0=0.6$). In a sample of 12 voters, only 3 support it. Test at the 5% level whether support is less than 60%, using $P(X\leq3)\approx0.0153$ for $X\sim B(12,0.6)$.
questions.target: Further binomial proportion tests
questions.answer: $H_0:p=0.6$. $H_a:p<0.6$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\leq3)=0.0153$. Since $0.0153<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that support is less than 60%.
questions.explanation: $H_0:p=0.6$. $H_a:p<0.6$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\leq3)=0.0153$. Since $0.0153<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that support is less than 60%.

questions.q: In the website crash-rate test, describe what a Type I error would mean in context, and what a Type II error would mean.
questions.target: Type I and Type II errors, and significance level
questions.answer: A Type I error would mean concluding the crash rate has decreased when it actually hasn't (rejecting a true $H_0$) — wrongly crediting the software update. A Type II error would mean failing to detect a real decrease in the crash rate (failing to reject a false $H_0$) — missing genuine improvement from the update.
questions.explanation: A Type I error would mean concluding the crash rate has decreased when it actually hasn't (rejecting a true $H_0$) — wrongly crediting the software update. A Type II error would mean failing to detect a real decrease in the crash rate (failing to reject a false $H_0$) — missing genuine improvement from the update.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by the significance level of a hypothesis test, and state the probability of a Type I error in a test conducted at the 5% significance level.
questions.target: Type I and Type II errors, and significance level
questions.answer: The significance level $\alpha$ is the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (a Type I error), chosen in advance by the person conducting the test. At the 5% significance level, $\alpha=0.05$, so there is a 5% probability of a Type I error.
questions.explanation: The significance level $\alpha$ is the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (a Type I error), chosen in advance by the person conducting the test. At the 5% significance level, $\alpha=0.05$, so there is a 5% probability of a Type I error.

questions.q: A researcher conducts a test at $\alpha=0.10$ instead of the more common $\alpha=0.05$. Explain how this affects the probability of Type I and Type II errors, compared to using $\alpha=0.05$.
questions.target: Type I and Type II errors, and significance level
questions.answer: Using a larger $\alpha=0.10$ increases the probability of a Type I error (the rejection region is larger, so a true $H_0$ is more likely to be rejected by chance) but decreases the probability of a Type II error (it becomes easier to reject $H_0$, so a false $H_0$ is more likely to be correctly rejected) — there is a direct tradeoff between the two error types as $\alpha$ changes.
questions.explanation: Using a larger $\alpha=0.10$ increases the probability of a Type I error (the rejection region is larger, so a true $H_0$ is more likely to be rejected by chance) but decreases the probability of a Type II error (it becomes easier to reject $H_0$, so a false $H_0$ is more likely to be correctly rejected) — there is a direct tradeoff between the two error types as $\alpha$ changes.

questions.q: This question has four parts. A factory's current process produces components with mean breaking strength $\mu_0=250$ N and known $\sigma=20$ N. A new process gives a sample of $n=40$ components with mean $\bar{x}=257$ N. (a) State $H_0$ and $H_a$ for testing whether the new process increases mean breaking strength (one-tailed). (b) Compute the test statistic $z$. (c) Using critical value $z^*=1.645$ (5% level), state the conclusion. (d) Quality control also monitors defects; the historical rate is $\lambda_0=5$ per batch, but a batch from the new process has only 1 defect. Using $P(X\leq1)\approx0.0404$ for $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(5)$, test at the 5% level whether the new process has reduced the defect rate.
questions.target: A well-designed word problem: testing a new manufacturing process
questions.answer: (a) $H_0:\mu=250$. $H_a:\mu>250$. (b) $z=\frac{257-250}{20/\sqrt{40}}=\frac{7}{3.1623}\approx2.214$. (c) Since $2.214>1.645$, we reject $H_0$: significant evidence at the 5% level that the new process increases mean breaking strength. (d) $H_0:\lambda=5$, $H_a:\lambda<5$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\leq1)=0.0404<0.05$, so we reject $H_0$: significant evidence at the 5% level that the new process has reduced the defect rate.
questions.explanation: (a) $H_0:\mu=250$. $H_a:\mu>250$. (b) $z=\frac{257-250}{20/\sqrt{40}}=\frac{7}{3.1623}\approx2.214$. (c) Since $2.214>1.645$, we reject $H_0$: significant evidence at the 5% level that the new process increases mean breaking strength. (d) $H_0:\lambda=5$, $H_a:\lambda<5$. $p\mathrm{-value}=P(X\leq1)=0.0404<0.05$, so we reject $H_0$: significant evidence at the 5% level that the new process has reduced the defect rate.

questions.q: The scores on a standardized test are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. A new scoring algorithm is implemented, and the scores are transformed using the rule $Y = aX + b$, where $X$ is the original score and $Y$ is the new score. The new distribution of scores, $Y$, also follows a normal distribution with a mean of 120 and a standard deviation of 22.5. Calculate the value of $a$ and the value of $b$.
questions.target: Further Poisson mean tests
questions.answer: Let $X \sim N(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)$ and $Y \sim N(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2)$. We are given $\mu_X = 100$, $\sigma_X = 15$, $\mu_Y = 120$, and $\sigma_Y = 22.5$. The linear transformation is given by $Y = aX + b$. We know that for a linear transformation $Y = aX + b$, the mean of $Y$ is $\mu_Y = a\mu_X + b$ and the standard deviation of $Y$ is $\sigma_Y = |a|\sigma_X$. From the standard deviation relationship: $\sigma_Y = |a|\sigma_X$ $22.5 = |a| \times 15$ $|a| = \frac{22.5}{15} = 1.5$ Now consider the mean relationship: $\mu_Y = a\mu_X + b$ $120 = a \times 100 + b$ We need to consider two cases for $a$: $a=1.5$ or $a=-1.5$. Case 1: $a = 1.5$ $120 = 1.5 \times 100 + b$ $120 = 150 + b$ $b = 120 - 150 = -30$ This gives $a=1.5$ and $b=-30$. Case 2: $a = -1.5$ $120 = -1.5 \times 100 + b$ $120 = -150 + b$ $b = 120 + 150 = 270$ This gives $a=-1.5$ and $b=270$. Looking at the choices, option A matches Case 1: $a = 1.5, b = -30$. Option B matches Case 2: $a = -1.5, b = 270$. Without further information or context (e.g., that the transformation should stretch the score range or map it in a specific direction), both could be mathematically valid based on the provided information. However, in most practical scenarios of score transformation for standardization or scaling, the coefficient $a$ is positive unless explicitly stated otherwise for a reflection or inversion. Assuming a standard scaling transformation where the order of scores is preserved, $a$ would be positive. If we consider the common practice of scaling where higher original scores map to higher new scores, we would assume $a>0$, which leads to $a=1.5$.
questions.explanation: Let $X \sim N(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)$ and $Y \sim N(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2)$. We are given $\mu_X = 100$, $\sigma_X = 15$, $\mu_Y = 120$, and $\sigma_Y = 22.5$. The linear transformation is given by $Y = aX + b$. We know that for a linear transformation $Y = aX + b$, the mean of $Y$ is $\mu_Y = a\mu_X + b$ and the standard deviation of $Y$ is $\sigma_Y = |a|\sigma_X$. From the standard deviation relationship: $\sigma_Y = |a|\sigma_X$ $22.5 = |a| \times 15$ $|a| = \frac{22.5}{15} = 1.5$ Now consider the mean relationship: $\mu_Y = a\mu_X + b$ $120 = a \times 100 + b$ We need to consider two cases for $a$: $a=1.5$ or $a=-1.5$. Case 1: $a = 1.5$ $120 = 1.5 \times 100 + b$ $120 = 150 + b$ $b = 120 - 150 = -30$ This gives $a=1.5$ and $b=-30$. Case 2: $a = -1.5$ $120 = -1.5 \times 100 + b$ $120 = -150 + b$ $b = 120 + 150 = 270$ This gives $a=-1.5$ and $b=270$. Looking at the choices, option A matches Case 1: $a = 1.5, b = -30$. Option B matches Case 2: $a = -1.5, b = 270$. Without further information or context (e.g., that the transformation should stretch the score range or map it in a specific direction), both could be mathematically valid based on the provided information. However, in most practical scenarios of score transformation for standardization or scaling, the coefficient $a$ is positive unless explicitly stated otherwise for a reflection or inversion. Assuming a standard scaling transformation where the order of scores is preserved, $a$ would be positive. If we consider the common practice of scaling where higher original scores map to higher new scores, we would assume $a>0$, which leads to $a=1.5$.

sections.heading: Part VI — Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (38–45)

questions.q: Describe the locus $|z-(2i)|=1$ in the Argand diagram. Find its radius.
questions.target: A well-designed word problem: testing a new manufacturing process

questions.q: A sequence satisfies $u_{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}u_n+8$ with $u_1=5$. Find $u_{3}$.
questions.target: The logic of hypothesis testing
questions.answer: Applying the recurrence 2 times from $u_1=5$ gives $u_{3}=\frac{53}{4}$.
questions.explanation: Applying the recurrence 2 times from $u_1=5$ gives $u_{3}=\frac{53}{4}$.

questions.q: Differentiate $y=(x)^{2}$ and evaluate $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at $x=0$.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a population mean (known σ)
questions.answer: $\frac{dy}{dx}=2\times 1\times (x)^{1}$. At $x=0$: $(x)=0$, giving $0$.
questions.explanation: $\frac{dy}{dx}=2\times 1\times (x)^{1}$. At $x=0$: $(x)=0$, giving $0$.

questions.q: Given that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $P(x)=4x^{3}-3x^{2}-x+m$, find the value of $m$.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a Poisson mean
questions.answer: By the Factor Theorem: $P(-3)=0 \Rightarrow -132+m=0\Rightarrow m=132$.
questions.explanation: By the Factor Theorem: $P(-3)=0 \Rightarrow -132+m=0\Rightarrow m=132$.

questions.q: Line $l_1:\mathbf{r}=(0,7,-2)+t(-1,1,-2)$ and line $l_2:\mathbf{r}=(-1,4,6)+s(1,1,-3)$ intersect at one point. Find the z-coordinate of the point of intersection.
questions.target: Further Poisson mean tests
questions.answer: The lines meet at $t=-1$, giving the point $(1,6,0)$. z-coordinate: 0.

questions.q: Given $\tan\theta=\frac{5}{3}$ with $\theta$ in Quadrant III, state the sign of $\sec\theta$.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a binomial proportion
questions.answer: Quadrant III: $\cos\theta$ is negative, so $\sec\theta$ is negative.
questions.explanation: Quadrant III: $\cos\theta$ is negative, so $\sec\theta$ is negative.
